summary: To weigh, above all to weigh out silver in payment, since silver changed hands by weight on the scales (Gen 23:16; Jer 32:9–10). The shekel (שֶׁקֶל) is the weight by which silver, gold, bronze and food were reckoned, fixed “by the shekel of the holy place” at twenty gerahs (Exo 30:13; Lev 27:25), and מִשְׁקָל is the weight of a thing, or a ration given by weight. Weighing is also judgment: Job asks to be weighed in balances of righteousness (Job 31:6), and the Aramaic of Daniel 5 reads תְּקֵל, “you have been weighed in the balances and found lacking” (Dan 5:27). Arabic ṯaqula “be heavy” and ṯiql “weight”, Ugaritic ṯql “shekel” and Akkadian šaqālu “weigh, pay” carry the same sense.

words.gloss: shekel: a weight, and silver reckoned by it
words.summary: “That which is weighed”: the standard weight of the balance. It weighs bronze and iron (1Sa 17:5, 7), hair (2Sa 14:26), spices (Exo 30:24) and bread (Ezk 4:10), but most often silver, so that a number of shekels of silver is a price. Scripture's shekels are weights, not stamped coins: the silver is weighed out on the scales (Jer 32:9–10).

senses.definition: The standard weight by which a thing is weighed: of bronze armour, an iron spearhead, a man's hair, spices, or a daily ration of bread.

evidence.note: “The weight (מִשְׁקַל) of the coat was five thousand שְׁקָלִים of bronze”: the shekel as the unit of מִשְׁקָל.
Goliath's spearhead was “six hundred shekels of iron”.
Absalom “weighed (וְשָׁקַל) the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's stone”: verb, noun and the weight-stone together.
Cassia, five hundred “by the shekel of the holy place”.
“Your food … by weight (בְּמִשְׁקוֹל), twenty shekels a day.”
“The weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold.”

The redemption price of a firstborn, “five shekels of silver by the shekel of the holy place”.
The princes' silver basins, “seventy shekels by the shekel of the holy place”.
In the prophet's ordinances for the land: “the shekel shall be twenty gerahs”, after the command for just balances (45:10).

words.summary: Twenty-one times. In most uses the thing weighed is silver or gold handed over, so that “weigh out” is “pay”: the price of a field, a bride price, a ransom, a bribe, a hire. The scales are named beside it (Jer 32:10; Job 6:2; 31:6; Isa 40:12).

senses.definition: To find or set the weight of a thing on the scales: hair, mountains, silver.

evidence.note: Absalom “weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's stone”.
“Who … weighed (וְשָׁקַל) the mountains in a scale (בַּפֶּלֶס) and the hills in a balance (בְּמֹאזְנָיִם)?”
“I weighed the silver on the scales (בְּמֹאזְנָיִם).”
“If only my vexation were weighed (שָׁקוֹל יִשָּׁקֵל), and my calamity laid in the balances together!” (the infinitive).

senses.definition: To hand over silver or gold by weight: a price, a bride price, a ransom, wages, a bribe, a gift to the house of God.

evidence.note: “Abraham weighed out to Ephron the silver that he had named … four hundred shekels of silver, current with the merchant.”
“I bought the field … and weighed out to him the silver, seven shekels and ten pieces of silver.”
If her father refuses, “he shall weigh out silver like the bride price of virgins”.
“Your life shall be for his life, or you shall weigh out a talent of silver”: pay a ransom.
“Though I should weigh out on my palms a thousand pieces of silver, I would not put out my hand against the king's son.”
“Give me my wages … and they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver”; Yahweh calls it “the magnificent price at which I was valued by them” (11:13).
“They weighed out (ἔστησαν) to him thirty pieces of silver”: the Septuagint's word for וַיִּשְׁקְלוּ at Zec 11:12.
“Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread, and your labour for what does not satisfy?”
“They weigh silver on the beam (בַּקָּנֶה), hire a goldsmith, and he makes it a god.”
Haman: “I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver … into the king's treasuries” to destroy the Jews; again 4:7.
Ezra “weighed out to them the silver and the gold and the vessels, the offering for the house of our God”; again 8:26.
“Guard them until you weigh them before the chiefs … in the chambers of the house of Yahweh.”
“Where is he who counted? Where is he who weighed?”: the oppressor's tribute officers, gone.

senses.definition: Of God trying a man as on the scales, to know his true worth.

“On the fourth day the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed in the house of our God.”

words.summary: Twice, both beside קַו “measuring line”, and both figurative: Yahweh's standard laid against a city. Spelled מִשְׁקֹלֶת at 2Ki 21:13. A weight hung on a line, as Syriac ܡܬܩܘܠܬܐ “weight; plummet”; whether it tested the upright or the level the two verses do not say.

words.summary: The third word of the writing on Belshazzar's wall, the Aramaic form of שֶׁקֶל. Daniel reads it by its verb: תְּקֵל, תְּקִילְתָּה “weighed: you have been weighed”, as he reads מְנֵא by מְנָה “numbered” and פְּרֵס by פְּרִיסַת “divided” (Dan 5:26–28).

senses.definition: The word written by the hand on the wall, which Daniel interprets as the king's weighing in God's balances.

doctrine.statement: Israel was commanded, “You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measure, in weight (בַּמִּשְׁקָל) or in quantity; just balances, just weights … I am Yahweh your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:35–36), and “a full and just weight you shall have, that your days may be long in the land” (Deu 25:13–15). “A false balance is an abomination to Yahweh, but a full weight is his delight”; “a just balance and scales are Yahweh's, all the weights of the bag are his work” (Pro 11:1; 16:11). The sanctuary's own shekel was fixed at twenty gerahs, the same for every valuation (Exo 30:13; Lev 27:25), and the half-shekel was the same for rich and poor (Exo 30:15). Amos condemns those who “make the ephah small and the shekel great, and falsify balances of deceit”, and Yahweh swears, “I will never forget any of their deeds” (Amo 8:5, 7). In the prophet's ordinances for the land the command is given again: “you shall have just balances … the shekel shall be twenty gerahs” (Ezk 45:10, 12). From the verses: honest weight is a matter of Yahweh's judgment, not of trade alone; to tamper with the shekel is to wrong the poor and to sin against him.

Yahweh is the one who “weighed the mountains in a scale and the hills in a balance” (Isa 40:12), before whom “the nations are as … the dust on the balances” (Isa 40:15). Job asks, “let him weigh me in balances of righteousness, and let God know my integrity” (Job 31:6). Belshazzar, who drank from the vessels of Yahweh's house and praised gods of silver and gold, “and the God in whose hand is your breath … you have not glorified”, was told, “you have been weighed in the balances and found lacking”, and “in that night Belshazzar … was slain” (Dan 5:23, 27, 30). Hannah says the same in other words: “Yahweh is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed” (1Sa 2:3). From the verses: God tests a man as silver is tested on the scales, by a true standard, and the judgment follows the weighing.

The law set thirty shekels of silver as the price of a servant gored by an ox (Exo 21:32). The shepherd of Zec 11 asked for his wages, “and they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver”, and Yahweh said, “throw it to the potter, the magnificent price at which I was valued by them”; and he threw it into the house of Yahweh, to the potter (Zec 11:12–13). Judas asked the chief priests, “what will you give me?”, “and they weighed out (ἔστησαν) to him thirty pieces of silver” (Mat 26:15); he threw the silver into the temple, the priests bought the potter's field with it, and Matthew says that the prophet's word was then fulfilled (Mat 27:5–10). From the verses: the price weighed out for Jesus was the price of a servant, and in the prophet it is the value set on Yahweh himself through his shepherd, so that their rejection of Jesus was their rejection of the God who sent him.

note: Drafted 2026-11-19. Root key שקל; BDB keys assigned: v.fq.aa verb, v.fq.ab שֶׁקֶל, v.fq.ac מִשְׁקוֹל, v.fq.ad מִשְׁקָל, v.fq.ae מִשְׁקֶלֶת; Biblical Aramaic xw.ag.aa תְּקַל (verb) and xw.ag.ab תְּקֵל (noun), root תקל. BDB's two Aramaic keys count the same three Dan 5:25, 27 tokens; here the verb takes the peil תְּקִילְתָּה (Dan 5:27) and the noun the two written תְּקֵל. Left unassigned: m.dy.af, a zero-token cross-reference (“מִשְׁקָל … see שׁקל”); v.fq.af שִׁקְמָה “sycamore” (7 tokens), filed next to this root by BDB but spelled שקמ, another root (Syriac ܫܩܡܐ, Arabic sawqam), left for an entry of its own. Already elsewhere: none of this root's words is in another entry (keseph, gadal, reva and be only quote שֶׁקֶל in phrases). No personal names: TIPNR has none from the root; Ashkelon (אַשְׁקְלוֹן) is a place and its tie to the root is unknown. The Peshitta's שקל “take up, bear” (SEDRA root 1923) has Syriac š, which answers Hebrew ש from *š, not this root's ṯ (Syriac ܬܩܠ), so it is another root; the Peshitta's ܬܩܠ/ܬܘܩܠܬܐ “stumble, stumbling block” (SEDRA root 1989, lexemes 3426–3427) is Jastrow's separate תְּקַל II “stumble” and is left out; whether “stumble” grew from “be heavy” is a question, not evidence. Arabic شقل (š, which answers Hebrew שׂ) and سقل were tried and left out. Mat 16:9 ← 1Sa 17:5 in the brief's quotation list is a false alignment. Open questions: (1) whether שֶׁקֶל is a loan from Akkadian šiqlu, as some argue, rather than inherited; Ugaritic ṯql and Arabic ṯiql with the regular ṯ point to an inherited word, recorded as cognate. (2) whether מִשְׁקֶלֶת is a plummet (upright) or a level (horizontal); Syriac ܡܬܩܘܠܬܐ “plummet” is cited from Wiktionary only, since Payne Smith's OCR is unreadable here and was not checked. (3) Ge'ez säqälä “hang” is recorded as possible; CAD for šaqālu “suspend” not checked. (4) The doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review.
